desc:
Implement file-name style globbing. The pattern pattern is made of the following elements, and the pattern has to match the entire string s:

  • a lowercase letter or digit matches exactly itself;
  • ? matches any single character;
  • * matches any sequence of characters, including the empty one;
  • a class [...] matches one character from a set. Inside the brackets there is a list of members, each either a single character (a lowercase letter or digit) or a range x-y meaning every character from x to y inclusive (x ≤ y, both of the same kind: letters with letters or digits with digits). If the very first character after [ is ^, the class is negated: it matches any single character that is not in the set.

Classes are never empty and never nested; - appears only as a range operator between two members, and ] only as the end of a class. The pattern is always well formed.

Examples: s = "hello3" matches h[a-f]llo? and *[0-9] and [^xyz]*, but does not match h[^e]llo3 or hello.
constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1,000, lowercase letters and digits only
1 ≤ pattern.length ≤ 500, made of lowercase letters, digits and the characters ? * [ ] ^ -
The pattern is well formed as described
hints: Compare with the plain wildcard problem (? and *): the new part is only that one pattern element can now match a set of characters. First turn the pattern into a list of elements, where a class is one element.
Write a helper matches(element, ch) for single-character elements (a literal, ?, or a class). Then use the standard two-pointer wildcard scan or a DP over (string position, element index).

For the two-pointer scan remember the last * and the string position where it started matching. On a mismatch, jump back to the star, let it absorb one more character and retry. At the end only stars may remain in the pattern.
editorial: First tokenize the pattern into a list of elements: a star, a question mark, a literal, or a class holding its negation flag and its list of ranges (a single member is a range of length one). Parsing a class is a short loop: after an optional ^, read members until ], treating x-y as a range when the next character is a dash.

Matching one character against an element is then trivial: a literal compares equal, ? always succeeds, and a class succeeds when the character is in one of the ranges, flipped by the negation flag. With that helper, the classic greedy wildcard algorithm applies. Walk through the string; if the current element is a star, remember its index and the current string position, and skip the star; if the element matches the current character, advance both; otherwise, if a star was seen, backtrack to it, advance the remembered string position by one and resume right after the star; otherwise fail. Once the string is consumed, skip trailing stars and succeed only if the whole pattern was used.

Only the most recent star ever needs to be retried, which is why the greedy method is correct. The worst case is O(n * m) for string length n and pattern length m, about 500,000 steps for the largest inputs here. A dynamic programming table over (position, element) gives the same bound with O(n * m) memory.
